name: Coptic
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Target list for Coptic holds one title, Säve-Söderbergh 1949 (Studies in the Coptic Manichaean Psalm-book: Prosody and Mandaean Parallels). It is a verse-metrics study (accent-group scansion of the Manichaean psalms, 3:3 rhythm, Mandaean parallels), not a description of word-stress placement, so: prosody-but-not-word-stress. No open copy exists: the two archive. acquisition priority low. What could be read: Guillaumont's 1950 RHR review (Persée, pp. 235-237 in full, saved) describes the metrical principle without any stress-placement rule; Drower's 1950 JRAS review is paywalled (DOI recorded). Best first-hand statement actually read in this sweep is Peust 1999 §6.1.6 p. 273 (already on file from the earlier audit pass): stress always on one of the last two syllables, position lexical/philologically recovered, phonemic status open; Steindorff 1904 §73 and Mallon 1907 §12 (on file) say the same. Note: the target file marks copt1239 as not in the catalog, but the tree holds an audit422 round-2 Coptic record (verdict 'S2 SCOPE-EXIT(lexical)') resting on exactly this Peust passage, and the egyp1246 catalog record is a back-projection of it; nothing found here changes that coding. All fetched sources material and the bibliographic records are under with lines added to.

new_statements.quote: Coptic words are always stressed on one of the last two syllables. Since Coptic word stress is intermingled with vowel quality and quantity to a high degree, it depends a lot on the interpretation of the vowel system whether stress in Coptic is to be considered bound or free. [...] (p. 270, sec. 6.1.2:) Fortunately, internal evidence of Coptic clearly indicates that exactly one syllable in a word is marked. [...] The short vowels H, O, and W can occur at most once in a word, i.e. in the marked syllable. [...] Long (i.e. double) vowels only appear in the marked syllable
new_statements.citation: Peust, Carsten. 1999. Egyptian Phonology: An Introduction to the Phonology of a Dead Language (Monographien zur Ägyptischen Sprache 2). Göttingen: Peust & Gutschmidt.
new_statements.locator: ch. 6 Prosody, sec. 6.1.6 'Phonemic stress in Coptic?', p. 273 (PDF page 273); supporting evidence sec. 6.1.2, p. 270
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

At sec. 6.1.6 'Phonemic stress in Coptic?', p. 273, the text reads exactly: 'Coptic words are always stressed on one of the last two syllables. Since Coptic word stress is intermingled with vowel quality and quantity to a high degree, it depends a lot on the interpretation of the vowel system whether stress in Coptic is to be considered bound or free. Cf. the following possible (near-)minimal pairs from Sahidic:...' The supporting lines at sec. 6.1.2 p. 270 are also there verbatim ('Fortunately, internal evidence of Coptic clearly indicates that exactly one syll…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every native Coptic word has exactly one stressed syllable, which is always the final or the penultimate syllable; the stressed syllable is the only one that can host the full vowels eta/o/omega and long (double-written) vowels, unstressed syllables having reduced e/schwa, so stress position is recoverable from vowel quality (two-syllable final window; whether 'bound' or 'free' depends on whether schwa is treated as a phoneme; Knudsen 1962 treats stress as non-phonemic).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; Peust p. 154 fn. mentions a suggestion that Coptic may have had intermediate degrees of stress; proclitic/construct-state elements are destressed (Steindorff par. 76-78).
new_statements.exceptions: Greek loanwords: internal criteria do not apply, accentuation uncertain (sec. 6.1.5). Late Coptic pronunciation and Coptic loans in Egyptian Arabic retract stress from a word-final stressed vowel (sec. 6.1.3, p. 271). Compounds with non-final stress treated in sec. 6.2.2. Possible near-minimal pairs ('ahe 'age' vs a'he 'yes') discussed p. 273-274.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for native words; Steindorff 1904 par. 76 (p. 37) adds that syntactically bound groups (construct state + noun, proclitics) are pronounced as one phonetic word with the stress on the last word, i.e. the domain is the bound group. Language is extinct; evidence is orthographic vowel distribution, manuscript accent marks, Late Coptic reading tradition and Arabic loans.
new_statements.identity_note: Peust 1999 describes Coptic across dialects (examples mainly Sahidic and Bohairic) and states explicitly (sec. 6.1.5, p. 273) that stress position is assumed not to vary across Coptic dialects or diachronically from Paleo-Coptic on. Steindorff 1904 and Mallon 1907 describe Sahidic/Bohairic respectively but give the same rule. Statement applies to native Coptic words; Greek loanwords are treated separately.

new_statements.quote: Coptic words are always stressed on one of the last two syllables. Since Coptic word stress is intermingled with vowel quality and quantity to a high degree, it depends a lot on the interpretation of the vowel system whether stress in Coptic is to be considered bound or free. Cf. the following possible (near-)minimal pairs from Sahidic: [ⲁϩⲉ 'age' vs. ⲉϩⲉ/ⲁϩⲉ 'yes'; ⲟⲩⲗⲗⲉ 'music' vs. ⲃⲗⲗⲉ 'blind'] As long as the unstressed -ⲉ is transcribed as /ə/ as it is here and everywhere in this book, these are not minimal pairs.
new_statements.citation: Peust, Carsten. 1999. Egyptian Phonology: An Introduction to the Phonology of a Dead Language (Monographien zur Ägyptischen Sprache 2). Göttingen: Peust & Gutschmidt. (author-released open access; already on file from the earlier audit pass)
new_statements.locator: § 6.1.6 'Phonemic stress in Coptic?', p. 273 (PDF page = printed page); cf. § 6.1.2 p. 270 and § 6.1.5 p. 273
new_statements.reading: One culminative stress per word, confined to the final two syllables (ultima or penult); which of the two is a word-by-word fact recovered philologically (§6.1.5), not a positional or weight rule, and its phonemic status depends on the vowel analysis (Knudsen 1962 non-phonemic; Peust leaves it open). Corroborated first-hand by Steindorff 1904 §73 p. 36 ('Jedes koptische, echtägyptische Wort hat nur einen betonten Vokal (Bildungsvokal), der in der letzten oder vorletzten Silbe steht') and Mallon 1907 §12 p. 17 ('L'accent tonique est toujours à la dernière ou à l'avant-dernière syllabe'), both read in the on-disk scanned texts. Säve-Söderbergh 1949 adds nothing on placement that could be read.

sources.note: Ch. 6 Prosody, sec. 6.1 Word stress (pp. 269-274): exactly one syllable per word is marked/stressed (evidence: eta, o, omega and long vowels occur only in that syllable; Bohairic aspirates contrast only in its onset), p. 270; 'Coptic words are always stressed on one of the last two syllables', whether bound or free depends on vowel analysis; Knudsen 1962 analyses it as non-phonemic (p. 273-274); Late Coptic/Arabic loans retract stress from word-final stressed vowels (p. 271).

sources.citation: Steindorff, Georg. 1904. Koptische Grammatik mit Chrestomathie, Wörterverzeichnis und Literatur. 2. Aufl. Berlin: Reuther & Reichard.
sources.note: Sec. 7 Betonung, par. 73-78 (pp. 36-37): 'Jedes koptische, echtägyptische Wort hat nur einen betonten Vokal (Bildungsvokal), der in der letzten oder vorletzten Silbe steht. Der Ton des Wortes ruht auf dieser Silbe'; other syllables have reduced e or schwa; par. 75 stress shifts to keep within last two syllables when suffixes added; par. 76 syntactic groups form one stress unit stressed on the last word.

sources.quote: Mais il est infiniment plus difficile de préciser les lois qui président à ce rythme. Il ne faut pas se dissimuler la part d'incertitude qui entre, en particulier, dans la détermination des éléments rythmiques, c'est-à-dire des mots qui se groupent sous un même accent métrique. Et c'est là pourtant une pièce de base du système. [...] Le rythme régulier est ici 3 : 3, et c'est la mesure caractéristique des hymnes mandéens. [EN: But it is infinitely harder to state the laws governing this rhythm. One must not hide the share of uncertainty that enters, in particular, into determining the rhythmic elements, i.e. the words that group under a single metrical accent. Yet that is a basic piece of the system. ... The regular rhythm here is 3:3, the characteristic measure of the Mandaean hymns.]
sources.note: Describes Säve-Söderbergh's system as accent-group (stress-count) verse scansion, 3:3 in the Psalms of Thomas; says nothing about where word stress falls in Coptic words.

sources.note: Not read (text not obtainable). From the two open reviews read (Guillaumont 1950 RHR pp. 235-237, in full; Drower 1950 JRAS, landing page only) the book is a metrical analysis of the Manichaean Psalm-book: verse lines are counted in 'éléments rythmiques, c'est-à-dire des mots qui se groupent sous un même accent métrique' (accent groups), regular rhythm 3:3 in the Psalms of Thomas, with Mandaean parallels. The review mentions no rule for the placement of the Coptic word accent; the work presupposes Coptic word stress for scansion rather than describing it.
